title: Giving One Last Chance to People Who Arent Making the Grade
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece tackles the common leadership impulse to give an underperforming team member 'one last chance' rather than accepting the facts and moving on. The author argues most last chances don't produce lasting change, but if a leader insists on giving one, it needs structure: a clear one-or-done framing, a set of milestones rather than a single all-or-nothing test, and design input from the team member themselves. The piece closes by noting that a well-designed last chance puts the outcome fully in the team member's control, which is what makes it fair.
points: Nine times out of ten, the better call is accepting the facts and moving on -- last chances rarely produce lasting change.
A poorly designed last chance hinges on one metric, which produces an agonizing 'last-last chance' when the team member gets close but doesn't clear the bar.
Milestones, not one-shot tests, give leaders a clearer and fairer basis for the final decision.
The team member, not the leader, should propose the milestones -- ownership of the design creates ownership of the outcome.
quotes: Of course, nine times out of 10, the better choice is to accept the facts and move on from the team member. Last chances rarely result in lasting change.
Well-designed last chances are made up of milestones, not all-or-nothing tests.
In too many cases, the last chance is based on only one key metric or result. When the team member gets close to achieving the goal but can’t claim victory, the leader remains torn.
Lastly, last chances should be designed initially by the team member, not the leader.
Win or lose, the last chance is now fully in the control of the team member. This empowers them to do their best, to figure out what eluded them in the past, and to accept whatever outcome occurs.
